summary: Describes an approach to carrying out large-scale SNMP traffic measurements to learn how SNMP is used in practice, since typical usage patterns are unclear. It also covers exchange formats for traces of that traffic so researchers can share data. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Everyone uses SNMP, but few know how. This describes how to watch lots of network chatter, record it in a shared format, and learn from the results.

questions: how is snmp used in practice
snmp trace exchange format xml csv
subtitle: Collecting and sharing real-world SNMP usage data for research.

tldr.problem: SNMP is widely deployed but it remains unclear how it is actually used in production networks, what protocols versions are preferred, and what typical usage patterns occur.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5345 describes a systematic approach to capturing, converting, filtering, storing and analyzing SNMP traffic traces, along with standardized XML and CSV formats for sharing trace data between network operators and researchers.
tldr.outcome: These measurement techniques and exchange formats enable the research community to develop a better understanding of real-world SNMP deployment patterns.

today: RFC 5345 is Informational and documents the consensus of the IRTF Network Management Research Group (NMRG). The measurement approach and trace formats remain current for SNMP research and operational analysis.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SNMP has been the dominant protocol for network management since the late 1980s, and three major versions exist: SNMPv1, SNMPv2c, and SNMPv3. Despite its wide deployment, fundamental questions about how the protocol is actually used remain unanswered. Operations staff often make assumptions about typical SNMP usage patterns without experimental evidence.

Many published papers compare SNMP performance or analyze specific table retrieval approaches, but these comparisons typically rely on assumed usage patterns rather than measurements from real networks. RFC 5345 addresses this gap by recommending a systematic approach to collecting and analyzing SNMP traffic from production networks.
sections.eli5: SNMP is everywhere but people guess about how it's used. This RFC explains how to actually measure it and prove what you think is happening.

sections.title: Measurement Approach
sections.content:
The measurement process consists of five basic steps. First, raw traffic is captured using standard packet sniffers like tcpdump or Wireshark, writing pcap files of SNMP traffic (typically UDP ports 161 and 162). The RFC recommends capturing at least one full week of data to capture diurnal patterns and one weekly cycle.

Second, raw pcap files are converted into structured, human and machine-readable formats. The RFC defines a RELAX NG schema for representing all SNMP message details in XML, and a more compact comma-separated values (CSV) format that captures only the most essential information about each SNMP message. This conversion step also handles IP reassembly for fragmented messages and corrects checksums affected by hardware TCP/IP offloading.

Third, the converted traces are filtered to remove or anonymize sensitive information such as community strings, access control lists, and specific node identifiers. Fourth, the filtered traces are submitted to a repository for archival and retrieval. Finally, researchers create and execute analysis scripts against the stored traces to extract meaningful information.
sections.eli5: Record the packets, turn them into readable format, hide secret stuff, save it, then write scripts to learn from it.

sections.title: Analysis Questions
sections.content:
Trace analysis can answer many questions about real-world SNMP usage. Basic statistics include which protocol versions are actually deployed, which protocol operations are most common, message size distributions, error types, and usage of authentication and encryption mechanisms. Analysis can distinguish between standardized SNMP objects and proprietary, vendor-specific objects.

Researchers can investigate the balance between periodic polling and aperiodic bulk data retrieval, examine how tables are read (object-by-object, row-by-row, or multi-row approaches), measure concurrency levels of concurrent SNMP requests, and study whether trap-directed polling is actually deployed in practice. Additional analyses can identify the most popular MIB modules, detect usage of obsolete SNMP objects, understand message encoding patterns, and study how management applications handle counter discontinuities and row creation.
sections.eli5: You can answer questions like: do people use new SNMP or old SNMP? Do they do a little bit of polling or one big download? How big are the messages? Do any of these things break?

sections.title: XML and CSV Trace Formats
sections.content:
The XML format, defined in RELAX NG compact notation, captures all details of SNMP messages including version, PDU type, variable bindings, and even BER encoding information (tag, length, and value sizes). This format retains information about the original ASN.1/BER encoding to support message size analysis. The XML schema supports SNMPv1, SNMPv2c, and SNMPv3 messages including the security parameters used in SNMPv3.

The CSV format provides a lightweight alternative for cases where detailed analysis is not needed. Each line represents one SNMP message with timestamp, source and destination IP addresses and ports, message size, SNMP version, protocol operation type, request ID, error status and index, number of variable bindings, and then three elements per varbind (object name, type, and value). The RFC recommends that CSV readers convert SNMPv1 traps to SNMPv2c/SNMPv3 format for consistency.
sections.eli5: XML keeps every detail about each SNMP message so you can study it carefully. CSV is simpler and smaller if you just need the basics.

sections.title: Privacy and Repository Management
sections.content:
SNMP traces contain sensitive information including community strings (in SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c), usernames (in SNMPv3), network topology details, and potentially confidential management data. Traces should be encrypted when archived, and standard anonymization techniques can be applied to maintain lexicographic ordering for instance identifiers while protecting sensitive values.

The RFC recommends that raw pcap files be kept in permanent storage even after conversion to XML and CSV, since improvements to conversion tools may require going back to the original source. Metadata about each trace (location, time period, contact information, known events during collection) should be recorded and stored with the trace itself, potentially using online services that provide unique identifiers.
sections.eli5: Hide the passwords and company secrets before sharing traces. Keep the original recordings in case someone finds a better way to read them later.
